title: What Gets Published From a Small Study
scopeNote: This is the original's second experiment, the two thousand simulated studies, which is the part no diagram can replace. Alpha, beta and power as three moving areas on two sampling distributions, and the sample-size calculator for a target power, stay in the longer version. The warning about computing power after the fact is kept here as a caution rather than dropped, because it is an error this activity could otherwise encourage.
summary: Two thousand honest studies of an effect that is genuinely there. Every estimate is kept, the significant ones are marked, and the distribution as a whole lands on the truth while the significant subset overstates it, sometimes enormously and occasionally in the wrong direction.
learningObjectives: Define power as a property of a study design rather than of a result.
Explain how conditioning on significance exaggerates effects without biasing any individual study.
Recognise Type S errors, where a significant result points the wrong way.
Explain why replications of small significant studies so often come out smaller.
Explain why power computed after a study, from the effect it observed, adds nothing to its p-value.
interactionTypes: three live controls over the population effect and the study size
two thousand complete simulated studies, each with its own sample and t-test
a histogram of every estimate with the significant subset marked by fill
the truth and the published average marked on the same axis
a one-press comparison of the same effect studied at two sample sizes
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Every simulation runs in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Significant and non-significant studies are distinguished by solid fill against outline, not by colour, and the truth and the published average are distinguished by dash pattern as well as by colour and both are labelled on the figure. The figure description gives the range, both averages, the exaggeration ratio, the power and the number of wrong-sign studies, and a full written summary appears as text beneath the tiles, so the entire argument is available without reading the histogram. Counts are correctly singular or plural. The figure scrolls sideways rather than shrinking below legible label sizes on a narrow screen. Changes are announced through a polite live region. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Simulated and illustrative. Two thousand fictional studies per run. Nothing here is a real literature, a real effect or a published finding.
simulationNotes: Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals, so a given seed runs the identical two thousand studies. Each study draws two samples of n from standard normal populations separated by the true effect, computes a pooled standard deviation, an observed Cohen's d and a pooled t on 2n minus 2 degrees of freedom, and takes a two-tailed p from the incomplete beta function. A closed form using the noncentral t would give the same numbers faster, but the argument is that no individual study is biased, and that is only convincing if every study is actually run and shown. The exaggeration ratio uses the mean of the absolute observed d among significant studies, which is the quantity Gelman and Carlin define: averaging the signed values would let wrong-sign studies cancel against correct ones and would understate the distortion. Simulation runs on change rather than on input, because two thousand studies is real work and dragging a slider would re-run it on every pixel.
readmeTopic: why the significant results from small studies overstate effects even when everyone is honest
